title: CMA CGM
subtitle: Managing fleet carbon and profitability, 2023–2030.
html:
View full presentation · Canva ↗

Evaluating carbon and profitability together

This project uses CMA CGM’s fleet as a case to evaluate how speed and fuel choices affect route earnings, annual emissions, and carbon intensity over 2023–2030. It seeks a fleet configuration that balances service, cost, and decarbonization.

Comparing four operating scenarios

The model compares regular speed with marine fuel oil (MFO), slower sailing with one additional vessel, regular speed with biofuel, and regular speed with liquefied natural gas (LNG). It evaluates three route configurations: PRX, EX1, and CAGML.

The comparison considers service margin before capital expenditure, absolute annual CO2 emissions, and AER/CII-based carbon-intensity performance. This brings the additional capacity needed for slower sailing into the same decision as fuel cost and emissions.

Choosing by route

The presentation finds that the best-margin and lowest-emission options vary by route. Slow MFO provides both advantages in the EX1 comparison, while PRX and CAGML involve tradeoffs between higher margins and lower emissions.

Recommendations prioritize slow steaming, targeted LNG deployment, and selective biofuel use. They also call for fuel- and carbon-price stress tests, with chartering and vessel redeployment considered before new capital investment.

Why the project matters

Decarbonization changes speed, vessel requirements, and operating costs, so it belongs within network planning. The project brings financial, operational, and environmental measures into one decision framework, making tradeoffs visible before a fleet commitment.

This article summarizes the presentation’s scenarios and recommendations, not realized company performance.
